title: Vocabulary
description: Topic words, collocations, phrasal verbs, idioms and word families at B2–C1 – with flashcards, sorting and matching.
intro: Precise vocabulary is one of the clearest signs of a strong exam performance. Don’t just learn single words – learn the words they go with (collocations). Use the flashcards for quick revision and the other tasks to test yourself.

exercises.title: Core concepts deck
exercises.instruction: Read the term, try to explain it in your own words, then flip the card. Mark each card as “I know it” or “Not yet”. Cards you don’t know come back at the end.

cards.definition: false or inaccurate information that is shared without the intention to deceive
cards.example: A lot of health misinformation is spread by people who genuinely want to help.

cards.definition: false information that is deliberately created or spread to mislead people
cards.example: The government accused a foreign state of running a disinformation campaign.

cards.definition: the ability to access, analyse, evaluate and create media critically
cards.example: Media literacy should be taught in every school subject, not just in IT lessons.

cards.definition: an environment in which people mainly hear opinions that repeat and reinforce their own
cards.example: If you only follow people who agree with you, you can end up in an echo chamber.

cards.definition: a situation in which algorithms show users mainly content that matches their previous behaviour and views
cards.example: Personalised news feeds may put users in a filter bubble without them noticing.

cards.definition: content, especially a headline, designed mainly to attract clicks rather than to inform
cards.example: “You won’t believe what happened next” is a classic example of clickbait.

cards.definition: the trail of data you leave behind when you use the internet
cards.example: Employers sometimes check applicants’ digital footprint before inviting them to an interview.

cards.definition: adverts shown to particular users based on data about their behaviour, interests or location
cards.example: Targeted advertising is the main source of income for many free platforms.

cards.definition: the right of journalists and media to report without censorship or intimidation
cards.example: Press freedom is a cornerstone of any functioning democracy.

cards.definition: public expression that attacks or incites hatred against people because of characteristics such as religion, ethnicity or sexual orientation
cards.example: The platform has been criticised for not removing hate speech quickly enough.

cards.definition: the process of reviewing and removing user posts that break a platform’s rules or the law
cards.example: Content moderation is often done by a mix of algorithms and low-paid human workers.

cards.definition: a video, image or audio recording manipulated with AI to make someone appear to say or do something they did not
cards.example: A deepfake of the candidate circulated just days before the election.

exercises.title: Advanced terms deck
exercises.instruction: These C1 terms will make your speaking more precise. Explain each term before you flip the card, and try to use it in a sentence of your own.

cards.definition: a person or organisation that decides which information reaches the public, traditionally editors and journalists
cards.example: Social media has weakened the role of traditional gatekeepers such as newspaper editors.

cards.definition: an organised campaign designed to look like spontaneous support from ordinary people
cards.example: Hundreds of identical reviews suggested the company was astroturfing.

cards.definition: warning people in advance about manipulation techniques so they can recognise false information later
cards.example: Short prebunking videos can make viewers better at spotting emotional manipulation.

cards.definition: presenting two sides of an issue as equally valid when the evidence clearly supports one side
cards.example: Giving a climate-change denier equal airtime as a climate scientist creates false balance.

cards.definition: presenting news in a shocking or exaggerated way to attract attention
cards.example: The tabloid was accused of sensationalism in its coverage of the trial.

cards.definition: avoiding saying or publishing something out of fear of negative consequences
cards.example: Online abuse can lead to self-censorship among female journalists.

cards.definition: the gap between people who have access to digital technology and skills and those who do not
cards.example: The pandemic made the digital divide between pupils painfully visible.

cards.definition: a widespread, often exaggerated fear that something threatens society’s values or safety
cards.example: Some historians compare today’s fears about smartphones to earlier moral panics about comics or video games.

cards.definition: having so much information that it becomes difficult to understand an issue or make decisions
cards.example: Constant notifications contribute to information overload.

cards.definition: a one-sided feeling of closeness to a media figure who does not know you
cards.example: Influencers profit from the parasocial relationships their followers develop.

cards.definition: a person who reveals secret information about wrongdoing inside an organisation
cards.example: The whistle-blower leaked internal documents to journalists.

cards.definition: the principle that people should be able to understand how automated systems make decisions
cards.example: Regulators are demanding more algorithmic transparency from large platforms.

exercises.title: Verb + noun collocations
exercises.instruction: Match each verb with the phrase it naturally goes with. Each verb has only one correct partner.

pairs.right: viral
pairs.explanation: A video or post “goes viral” when it spreads very quickly online.

pairs.right: someone’s privacy
pairs.explanation: Paparazzi and data brokers can “invade someone’s privacy”.

pairs.right: the powerful to account
pairs.explanation: To “hold someone to account” = make them explain and take responsibility for their actions.

pairs.right: the news agenda
pairs.explanation: Media that “set the agenda” decide which topics people talk about.

pairs.right: confidential documents
pairs.explanation: To “leak” information = give secret information to the public or press.

pairs.right: a balance between freedom and safety
pairs.explanation: To “strike a balance” = find a fair compromise between two things.

pairs.right: public awareness
a clear line between ads and content
pairs.explanation: To “draw a line between” two things = make a clear distinction.

exercises.explanation: Collocations are word partnerships that native speakers use automatically. Saying “make a balance” or “do awareness” is understandable but sounds unnatural – examiners notice. Learn these as complete chunks.

exercises.title: Phrasal verbs for the digital world
exercises.instruction: Match each phrasal verb with its meaning. Then say an example sentence about media for each one.

pairs.right: take strong action to stop something
pairs.explanation: The government is cracking down on online scams.

pairs.right: choose not to take part in something
pairs.explanation: You can opt out of personalised advertising in the settings.

pairs.right: remove something, e.g. a post or website
pairs.explanation: The platform took down the video within an hour.

pairs.right: make something seem less important than it is
pairs.explanation: The company tried to play down the data breach.

pairs.right: support a claim with evidence
pairs.explanation: Can you back up that claim with a reliable source?

pairs.right: consider the advantages and disadvantages
pairs.explanation: Before you share a post, weigh up whether it could hurt someone.

pairs.right: find or see something by chance
pairs.explanation: I came across an interesting article about deepfakes.

pairs.right: stay informed about the latest developments
pairs.explanation: It’s hard to keep up with the news when it changes every hour.

exercises.explanation: Phrasal verbs make your speaking sound natural. In formal writing, you can often replace them with a single verb: crack down on → suppress, back up → support, play down → minimise.

exercises.title: From definition to word
exercises.instruction: Read each definition and choose the word it describes. Watch out: the wrong options are related words that mean something different.

questions.prompt: Publishing someone’s private information, such as their home address, online without consent, usually to harass them.
questions.explanation: Doxxing comes from “docs” (documents). Phishing tricks people into giving away passwords; trolling provokes; catfishing uses a fake identity.

questions.prompt: Creating a fake online identity to deceive someone, often in a romantic context.
questions.explanation: Catfishing = pretending to be someone else. Ghosting = suddenly ending all contact without explanation.

questions.prompt: Continuing to scroll through bad or upsetting news even though it makes you feel worse.
questions.explanation: Doomscrolling = doom (disaster) + scrolling. News avoidance is the opposite reaction: deliberately staying away from news.

questions.prompt: The tendency to look for and believe information that supports what you already think.
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is a psychological tendency inside each person. An echo chamber is an environment; groupthink is a group’s pressure to agree.

questions.prompt: Deliberately posting provocative or offensive messages to upset people and provoke reactions.
questions.explanation: Trolls want to provoke. Spamming = sending masses of unwanted messages; flagging = reporting content to a platform.

questions.prompt: A fraudulent message designed to trick people into revealing passwords or bank details.
questions.explanation: Phishing (from “fishing”) tries to make you “take the bait”. Spam is any unwanted bulk message; malware is harmful software.

questions.prompt: Reading content in an online community without ever posting anything yourself.
questions.explanation: A lurker reads but does not post. Most members of online communities are lurkers.

questions.prompt: A person whose job is to present information in a way that makes a politician or organisation look good.
questions.explanation: A spin doctor puts a positive “spin” on events. A whistle-blower reveals wrongdoing; a gatekeeper controls what gets published.

exercises.title: Spreading vs. fighting false information
exercises.instruction: Sort each expression into the correct category: does it describe a way of creating or spreading false information, or a way of fighting it?

items.text: take a quote out of context

items.explanation: cherry-pick = choose only the facts that support your view
debunk = show that something is false

items.text: trace a claim to its source

items.explanation: flag = report or mark something for attention

exercises.explanation: Strong verbs like fabricate, doctor, cherry-pick and debunk are much more precise than “make fake news” or “show it’s wrong”. Use them in your monologue.

exercises.title: Word families
exercises.instruction: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the word in capitals. You may need a prefix, a suffix or both. Type your answer and check it.

items.gapped: The ___ of online sources varies enormously.
items.explanation: Noun needed after “the … of”: rely → reliable → reliability.

items.gapped: Online ___ can encourage people to say things they would never say in person.
Many apps are deliberately designed to be highly ___.
Platforms should be held ___ for the content their algorithms promote.
The scandal seriously damaged the newspaper’s ___.
items.explanation: Noun after a possessive: credible → credibility.

items.gapped: No news outlet is ever completely ___.
items.explanation: The meaning requires a negative adjective: biased → unbiased (= impartial).

items.gapped: There is a worrying lack of ___ about how recommendation algorithms work.
Social media is often blamed for the growing ___ of society.
The claim turned out to be completely ___ – nobody could find any evidence for it.
items.explanation: The context (“nobody could find any evidence”) needs a negative adjective with -able: verify → verifiable → unverifiable.

exercises.title: Choose the precise word
exercises.instruction: All options look similar, but only one fits naturally in each sentence. Choose it, then read the explanation to understand why the others don’t work.

questions.prompt: The minister ___ the allegations as “fake news”.
questions.explanation: “Dismiss something as …” = reject it as not worth considering. “Refuse” is followed by an offer or a request, not by allegations.

questions.prompt: The video ___ millions of views within a single day.
questions.explanation: “Rack up” = collect a large number of something (views, points, debts).

questions.prompt: Journalists have a duty to protect their ___.
questions.explanation: A journalist’s “sources” are the people who give them information. Protecting sources is a core principle of journalism.

questions.prompt: Critics warn that the new law could have a ___ effect on free speech.
questions.explanation: A “chilling effect” = people stop expressing themselves because they fear consequences. It is a fixed expression.

questions.prompt: The story was blown out of ___ by the tabloids.
questions.explanation: “Blow something out of proportion” = make it seem much more serious than it is.

questions.prompt: There is a fine ___ between satire and misinformation.
questions.explanation: “There’s a fine line between X and Y” = the difference is very small.

questions.prompt: The influencer was accused of ___ her followers by not disclosing paid partnerships.
questions.explanation: To “mislead” someone = make them believe something untrue.

questions.prompt: Her post was taken ___ because it violated the community guidelines.
questions.explanation: “Take down” a post/website = remove it from the internet.

questions.prompt: The newspaper had to print a ___ after publishing false claims about the mayor.
questions.explanation: A newspaper “prints a correction” (or a retraction) when it has published something false.

exercises.title: Adverb + adjective power pairs
exercises.instruction: Strong adverb + adjective combinations make your arguments sound more convincing. Choose the adverb that collocates naturally in each sentence.

questions.prompt: Some apps are ___ addictive.
questions.explanation: “Highly addictive” is the standard collocation (also: highly effective, highly controversial).

questions.prompt: The decision was ___ criticised by human rights groups.
questions.explanation: “Heavily criticised” (or “widely criticised”). “Highly criticised” is a common learner mistake.

questions.prompt: The effects of social media on mental health remain ___ contested.
questions.explanation: “Hotly contested / debated” = argued about with strong feelings.

questions.prompt: Many parents are ___ concerned about cyberbullying.
questions.explanation: “Deeply concerned / worried / divided” express strong emotion.

questions.prompt: The leak was ___ reported in the international press.
questions.explanation: “Widely reported / known / used” = by many people or in many places.

questions.prompt: It was ___ obvious that the photo had been edited.
questions.explanation: “Glaringly obvious” = extremely obvious (also: blatantly obvious).

questions.prompt: Public opinion is ___ divided on the question of a social media ban.
questions.explanation: “Deeply divided” (also “sharply divided”) is the natural collocation.

exercises.title: Build your topic word map
exercises.instruction: Sort the terms into the four subtopics. This gives you a mind map of vocabulary you can use for different exam questions.
exercises.explanation: Organising vocabulary by subtopic helps you find the right words quickly in the exam. Add your own terms to each category in your notes.

exercises.title: Evaluating sources: positive or negative?
exercises.instruction: Sort the adjectives: would you use them to praise a source or to criticise it? These words are perfect for analysing a text or image in the exam.

items.explanation: strongly supporting one political party or side

exercises.explanation: Instead of saying a source is “good” or “bad”, say it is reputable, nuanced and well-sourced – or sensationalist, partisan and unsubstantiated.

exercises.title: Negative prefixes
exercises.instruction: Which prefix makes each word negative or gives it the meaning “wrongly”? Sort each word under the correct prefix.
exercises.explanation: Patterns: ir- before r (irrelevant), il- before l (illegal), im- before p/m (impossible). mis- means “wrongly” (misquote = quote wrongly). These are rules of thumb, not laws – always check a dictionary.

exercises.title: Phrases for structuring your talk
exercises.instruction: Sort the phrases by their function in a monologue. Then choose one phrase from each group and use it in your next speaking practice.
exercises.explanation: Signposting phrases help the examiner follow your argument. “Having said that” and “Admittedly … but” are especially useful because they show you can see both sides.

exercises.title: Idioms for media talk
exercises.instruction: Match each idiom with its meaning. Using one or two idioms correctly in the exam shows a high level – but don’t overdo it.

pairs.right: suddenly become widely reported in the news
join something because it is popular, not out of conviction

pairs.left: take something with a pinch of salt
pairs.right: not completely believe something
be famous and watched closely by the media
a small visible part of a much bigger problem
a lot of anger about something unimportant
understand a meaning that is not stated directly

pairs.left: bite the hand that feeds you
pairs.right: harm someone who supports or pays you

exercises.explanation: Example uses: “Brands jumped on the bandwagon of TikTok marketing.” – “Influencers who criticise their sponsors risk biting the hand that feeds them.” – “Reported cases of cyberbullying may be just the tip of the iceberg.”
